about: The Notebook's ledger: how Newspaper Night Sky was made, one dated entry at a time. Add an entry when something happens (a decision, a wrong turn, a difficulty overcome, a moment of care), not later from memory. The build (work/notebook_parts.py) renders notebook.html from it and checks every entry: its phase, its kinds and that its links open pages of the site. Quotes are the maker's own words, as written; edit or remove one only with the maker's OK.

phases.title: Beginnings · 27 October – 5 November
phases.intro: A dataset of 77,749 newspaper pages, a question about attention, and the decision to show what the papers printed rather than prove a large claim.

phases.title: Building the instruments · 6 – 8 November
phases.intro: The pulses, the sky, and learning how far the machine's reading of the papers can be trusted.

phases.title: Generosity and care · 9 November
phases.intro: A day of asking who the site is for: the visitor in front of it, everyone who visits, and the people named in the papers.

phases.title: Voices, reviews and the archive's own errors · 9 – 10 November
phases.intro: Recorded voices, five reviewed years, and an archive that turned out to misfile some of its own pages.

phases.title: Rethinking · 11 November
phases.intro: A hard question from the maker, and a day of testing ideas before building them.

entries.title: The question we started with
entries.text: Society has a limited amount of attention, and problems keep coming back. Does lasting change need sustained attention? The archive: American newspapers from 1770 to 1810, as the Smithsonian's Revolution Crossroads prepared them from the Library of Congress.

changed.label: Still asked
links: How things come back, on Findings

entries.title: Show what was printed; let visitors judge
entries.text: The share of a topic in the surviving papers is not the share of a society's attention, and the archive could not carry a proof of the big question. We chose an explorer of observed facts, “newspaper X printed this on date Y”, over a thesis.

changed.label: Changed
links: the whole site: instruments, not a verdict

entries.title: A count is a target, not a quota
entries.text: Some story groups were thin, and the pulses would have looked richer with a few more printings in them. The rule: never pad a thin group to make the animation look better. What the papers did not print stays unprinted.

entries.title: The transcription left out what the paper printed
entries.text: On 13 October 1797 the Gazette of the United States printed Captain Dunbar's full statement about a privateer; the archive's AI transcription simply dropped it, about 350 words. From then on, every reviewed printing was read against its page scan, and the misreadings are recorded beside the passages.

entries.title: Trust the transcriptions to find stories, not to quote them
entries.text: Reading every page by hand would take years. So the computer matched shared wording across all 41 years, 48,127 stories at first, kept apart from the stories checked by hand and labelled “not checked”.

entries.title: Time runs into the depth
entries.text: The maker's idea: look at the stories as at the night sky, where the farther a star, the older its light. The telescope was built around it the same day, and the project took its name, Newspaper Night Sky.

entries.title: Colouring the stars by kind
entries.text: We tried to colour stars as news, notices or other, from the topic model. A spot check found 2 or 3 of 14 “notices” right; a stricter cut still got 10 of 16. The colours would have told visitors something untrue, so they went.

changed.label: Changed
links: why topics are a layout, not a colour

entries.title: An inviting and generous portal

quote.text: are we really making an inviting and generous portal?

entries.text: The Pulses page asked visitors to choose from menus before it showed anything. It gave them up: a strip of all 41 years, each with how much of it survives, and a shelf of stories that shows what there is before anyone asks.

entries.title: Nobody pays for a visit

quote.text: for the user viewing the page, i do not want them to use my ai tokens

entries.text: The radio could have called an AI voice for each visitor. It uses the browser's own voice and sounds made in the page; every reviewed passage was recorded once, at build time, and plays from a file.

entries.title: For everyone who visits
entries.text: An accessibility pass over every page: a link to skip the menu, names for every control, contrast, targets of at least 24 pixels, keyboard paths through the sliding controls, and pages that still read at 320 pixels wide, all checked with a real keyboard.

entries.title: Names we did not print
entries.text: In 1776, Philadelphia's committees printed notices naming people who refused the Continental bills, 18 printings. They name private people, singled out in their own day. We left them out of the reviewed stories: they could become a story of their own later, with the context they need.
entries.source: The reviewed stories of 1776, second round

entries.title: A siren in 1776

quote.cite: the maker, hearing the radio's New York

entries.text: Each town got its own morning sound: church bells, a ship's bell, hooves, birds. New York got a police siren, a deliberate anachronism, and How it works says so.

entries.title: A chorus that murmured

quote.text: never be murmuring sounds or some random things

entries.text: Synthesised voices let many stars speak at once, and it sounded like a crowd, not news. They gave way to voices on demand, then to recordings made once with a free local model, and the synthesiser was removed.

entries.title: More than one kind of voice
entries.text: Nine readers, four women and five men, read the papers, and two hosts, a man and a woman, take turns introducing them.

entries.title: Twenty hours of recording, done by evening
entries.text: At half the speed of speech, recording the titles of 7,031 stories would have taken this laptop about twenty hours. Split into two recordings running side by side, they were done the same evening, with no failures.

changed.label: Changed
links: every story in four or more papers can be heard

entries.title: A newspaper filed two years late
entries.text: Reviewing 1808, the mastheads of the Kentucky Gazette said 1806. Every issue filed under 1806–1808 had been printed two years earlier: 106 issues. They were redated from their mastheads and matched again, and 4,506 new matches appeared.

entries.title: Pages filed under the wrong number
entries.text: One misplaced page in 1807 led to a check of the whole dataset: 133 issues had their machine transcriptions filed under the wrong pages. 532 printings were moved back to the scans they belong to, so a reader who opens a page now sees the text that is on it.

entries.title: Stories that wait for their context
entries.text: Some reports were not admitted to the reviewed stories yet, among them the act prohibiting the importation of slaves, news from Saint-Domingue and Haiti, and reports on the Cherokee and Creek nations. They are not left out for good: they wait until they can be shown with the framing they need.

changed.label: Waiting
changed.note: in the review notes of 1776, 1793 and 1807

entries.title: A rule that fits the evidence
entries.text: For 1793 only six to eight newspapers survive at a time, and only ten printed items reached the seven papers asked of other years. Rather than stretch the evidence or leave most of the year out, the threshold for 1793 became six, said openly.

entries.title: A deep logic behind the plans

quote.text: we need to have a deep logic behind the plans and strategy we made

entries.text: The controls had grown complex, and the reviews of them were shallow. Thinking again from first principles found the causes: two worlds of evidence, controls of different kinds mixed, one click with two meanings, and the tested findings hidden.

changed.label: Changed
links: one sky of stories, and select then act

entries.title: The source comes first

quote.text: help visitors build key frameworks or impressions of the source base instead of moving forward with some doubts

entries.text: So Findings opens with the archive itself: what survives and when, and how far the machine's reading can be trusted, before any pattern.

entries.title: A cycle of any length, tested first

quote.cite: the maker, suggesting cycles of a week, a month or any length

entries.text: A scan of every cycle from 6 to 400 days found only the year: weeks were the papers' printing days, months were echoes. So the idea was not built. What does come back irregularly, in waves, was: the embargo with every crisis, the war with Tripoli exactly.

entries.title: “1784–1789” was wrong
entries.text: The thin years were written from memory. Drawing the chart showed 1787 with ten newspapers: only 1784–1786 are thin. It was corrected on the live site the same day.
